There is a second reason this tour is timely. The repository rebuilt itself. Today’s live tree is kt-kernel, a slimmer C++/Python library whose README promises “CPU-optimized kernel operations for heterogeneous LLM inference” plus a fine-tuning track with LlamaFactory. The historic Python servers — the OpenAI-compatible API, the balance-serve scheduler, the old kvc2 prefix cache — now live under archive/, preserved but no longer the point. Reading the old tree to understand the new one wastes effort, so this walk sticks to the files that ship today. That also makes KTransformers a useful contrast to our DeepSpeed coverage: DeepSpeed moves tensors to CPU as an offload afterthought, while kt-kernel was designed around the CPU from the first line.

The map below shows the whole engine. A thin Python CLI and loader family hand weights to a pybind11 bridge; the bridge exposes operator interfaces implemented twice — once with Intel AMX tiles, once in portable AVX2 — while a paged KV cache serves Quest-style sparse attention, and a NUMA-aware worker pool keeps dozens of cores fed.

Overview of kt-kernel: the Python frontend and loaders feed the native bridge; operator interfaces dispatch to AMX or AVX2 expert kernels and the block-sparse attention path, all running over a NUMA worker pool, with CUDA ops handling GPU-side GPTQ and gating.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • kt run (run.py, L85) resolves a model, sanity-checks environment variables, and either boots the engine directly or builds a SGLang command that loads kt-kernel as its CPU expert backend — the same integration path our SGLang tour covered from the serving side.
  • The loader family in loader.py, L816 reads GGUF checkpoints (a format our llama.cpp tour traced back to its C++ origin) and a whole zoo of safetensor precisions, then translates tensor names into kt-kernel’s slots.
  • The native bridge (ext_bindings.cpp, L561) publishes the operator contracts from common.hpp, L418 and stamps __cpu_variant__ attributes onto the module so Python can pick AMX, AVX-512, or AVX2 code at import time.
  • On the GPU side, a separate extension (binding.cpp, L22) registers GPTQ Marlin GEMM, top-k softmax gating, and GGUF dequantization kernels — a vocabulary shared with vLLM, from which the gating kernel is explicitly adapted.
  • Underneath everything, task_queue.h, L22 and worker_pool.h, L138 provide the NUMA-aware execution fabric every kernel runs on.

Now let’s descend into each layer.

A Framework That Rebuilt Itself Around kt-kernel

The first surprise in the repo listing is how small the live surface is. archive/ holds several generations of the old project, including the C++ sources of the original KTransformers servers. The active tree is kt-kernel/, and its shape tells you the architecture story immediately: operators/ for the math, cpu_backend/ for threading, cuda/ for GPU helpers, python/ for the CLI and loaders, plus one top-level ext_bindings.cpp gluing it together.

The Python entry (run.py, L170) shows how deliberately thin the frontend is. _run_impl checks for conflicting environment variables (L586), picks between local serving and delegating to SGLang, and otherwise stays out of the way. This is the opposite philosophy from Triton Inference Server, which owns the whole serving surface; kt-kernel is a kernel library that deliberately lets a real server own the HTTP.

The import-time variant detection is the cleverest bridge detail. ext_bindings.cpp, L565 attaches attributes like "amx", "avx512_bf16", "avx512_vnni", and "avx2" to the module, alongside __int8_weight_layout__ at L583. Python code inspects these flags once and binds the right specialization, so no runtime dispatch tax is paid inside the hot loop. The config structs that flow through the bridge live in common.hpp, L143: a GeneralConfig baseline, QuantConfig at L222, GeneralMOEConfig at L230, and the two abstract contracts — MLA_Interface at L412 and MoE_Interface at L418 — that every backend implementation must satisfy. Nothing in the Python layer knows whether AMX or AVX2 will answer.

CPU MoE Experts: AMX Tiles and the CRTP Stack

The heart of kt-kernel is its mixture-of-experts execution on CPU, and the AMX path is the flagship. Intel’s Advanced Matrix Extensions add tile registers and TMUL dot-product instructions; exploiting them requires weights staged in exactly the right layout. The class hierarchy uses curiously-recurring templates: AMX_MOE_BASE, L39 provides the shared machinery, and each quantization flavor derives from it, while AMX_MOE_TP, L82 wraps per-NUMA-partition instances behind the tensor-parallel facade of TP_MOE at L427.

Weight loading is half the performance battle. load_weights, L263 repacks raw quantized expert bytes into the tile layout AMX demands, with integrity checks like verify_load_right at L154 to catch silent layout corruption. The B-side tile construction lives in amx_buffers.hpp, L499, where BufferBInt4Impl copies each 16×16 tile and applies the VNNI transpose (self-inverse, so the same routine handles both directions) visible at L704. On the A side, BufferAImpl, L20 stages activations with k-group variants for different block-quantized weight shapes.

The forward pass is two GEMMs. do_gate_up_gemm, L238 projects each token’s hidden state through the selected experts’ gate and up matrices, then applies SwiGLU in AVX-512 registers — the activation function sits in amx.hpp, L47, and init_tile at L157 configures the TMUL tile dtypes once per compute type. do_down_gemm, L251 finishes the expert FFN by projecting back down and accumulating into per-partition outputs. Because each NUMA partition owns its own experts’ weights, most memory traffic stays on one socket — which is exactly why the thread pool below matters so much.

For hosts without AMX — AMD EPYC machines, older Intel boxes — AVX2_MOE_BASE, L39 implements the same contract in portable intrinsics, with its own weight staging at L185. The release notes flag AVX2-only support as the path that brought AMD servers into LoRA fine-tuning, and the Python-side wrapper GeneralMoEWrapper, L29 is where a serving framework’s MoE layer gets bound to whichever backend the CPU supports.

Quest-Style Sparse Attention Over Paged KV

Long-context MoE models die on attention long before they die on experts, so kt-kernel’s second pillar is a block-sparse KV cache in the Quest style: keep the full cache, but let each decode step look closely at only the most promising blocks. The manager side is KVCache, L178, sized by KVCacheConfig, L111, with ThreadResize, BatchResize, and BlockResize entry points at L201 through L223 handling the three axes of concurrency.

The attention driver is attn_with_kvcache, L499, which selects between the layer-oriented and KV-head-oriented code paths (the latter starting at attention_kvhead_, L18 for multi-head variants). The sparse sequence then unfolds in four steps. First, quantize_q_, L532 compresses queries to integers so block scoring becomes cheap integer dot products. Second, calculate_block_similarity_layer_, L608 scores every cached block against those queries. Third, select_block_layer_, L737 keeps only the top blocks under the sparsity budget, and retrieval_kvcache_layer_, L799 gathers their K/V pages into a compact working set for the real (full-precision) attention kernel. Finally, calculate_sparsity_layer_, L849 records how much of the cache actually got touched, and get_attn_sparsity, L1514 exposes that number upward so schedulers can adapt budgets.

GPU readers of our FlashInfer tour will recognize the shape of this idea: approximate, structure-aware attention that trades a little recall for a large bandwidth win. The difference is substrate. FlashInfer optimizes what the GPU touches; kt-kernel optimizes what leaves DRAM at all, which on a CPU-bound hybrid stack is the resource that matters.

The NUMA Backend: Queues, Pools, Work Stealing

Every kernel above assumes a pool of workers that understand socket topology, and that fabric is worth its own section. ThreadState, L63 is the per-thread record — cache-line aligned with alignas(64) to stop false sharing, holding core and NUMA node ids plus scratch space. InNumaPool at L72 allocates those states from the right node, and NumaJobDistributor, L105 splits jobs across nodes so an expert computes on the socket that holds its weights.

The WorkerPool, L138 constructor wires it together, init at L159 pins threads, and the escape hatch for uneven work is do_work_stealing_job, L153: when the static NUMA split leaves one socket idling, its threads steal remaining indices from the busy one. Above the pool, TaskQueue, L22 offers the tiny API kernels actually use — enqueue at L27 to submit, sync at L29 to drain — keeping synchronization out of the kernel bodies.

From Install to Your First Model

Installation follows the kernel-library pattern — no service daemon, no config zoo:

git clone https://github.com/kvcache-ai/ktransformers.git
cd ktransformers/kt-kernel
pip install .

kt --help then reveals the CLI surface: run for serving, chat for interactive sessions, bench for throughput, doctor for hardware capability checks, plus quant and sft for the fine-tuning track. A minimal local launch looks like:

kt run --model-path /models/DeepSeek-R1-0528 --gguf-path /models/gguf

The loader negotiates precisions at startup. loader.py, L19 enumerates the GGML quantization types it understands, and the safetensor family covers the modern zoo: FP8 at L332, GPTQ at L1081, MXFP4 at L1198, NVFP4 at L1312, and MXFP8 at L1405. Name translation — mapping a checkpoint’s tensor names into kt-kernel’s expectations — is centralized in translate_name_to_gguf at L89, which is the single most useful file to read when a new model architecture lands.

GPU experts get their weights through the CUDA extension. binding.cpp, L94 registers gptq_marlin_gemm, backed by the warp-specialized Marlin kernel at gptq_marlin.cu, L60 — the same INT4 tensor-core design our vLLM tour saw in production — and binding.cpp, L97 registers topk_softmax, whose fused gating kernel (topkGatingSoftmax, L164) computes softmax, max, argmax, and top-k selection in one launch, adapted from vLLM’s kernels as the file header notes. The placement story this enables is exactly what the README advertises: hot experts on GPU, cold experts on CPU.

The fine-tuning track deserves its own tour, but the shape is worth knowing: KTransformers × LlamaFactory integration lets MoE experts stay quantized on CPU while LoRA adapters train on GPU, and the team reports 6-12× faster training than ZeRO-Offload baselines on the same hardware — a claim we flag as vendor-reported, not independently verified.

Honest Limits and Where kt-kernel Fits

Limits first, since they decide whether this tool belongs in your stack. It is x86-centric: the AMX path needs Sapphire Rapids-or-newer Intel, and while the AVX2 fallback widens coverage to AMD, ARM is off the table for the CPU side. The vendor list in cpu_backend/vendors/ hints at Ascend NPU and HIP ports, but the mature path is CUDA-plus-Intel-CPU. Attention sparsity is approximate — block scoring can miss what full attention would catch, so quality-sensitive deployments should measure, not assume. And the repository is mid-pivot: tutorials and tooling still straddle the old servers and the new kernel, so documentation occasionally points at archive/ paths that are no longer load-bearing.

As for fit: kt-kernel is the answer when model size, not request volume, is your constraint — the single-node case where a 600GB-class MoE model must serve a handful of users on hardware you already own. For multi-tenant serving with routing and batching at scale, the SGLang integration hands those problems to a dedicated server, and for cloud-scale deployments you would compare against the hosted paths in our inference overview or the serving-stack tours of Triton and MLC-LLM. Read it as a specialization of the same lesson llama.cpp taught: when the bottleneck is memory bandwidth, the cheapest spare memory in the building is usually the DIMMs you already have — and KTransformers shows what it takes to make those DIMMs fast.
entry.summary: A guided walk through the kt-kernel source tree: AMX and AVX2 expert kernels, Quest-style sparse attention, a NUMA worker pool, and the CUDA helpers that tie CPU and GPU together.

entry.title: Inside TurboMind: The C++ Engine Core of InternLM/lmdeploy

link.title: Inside TurboMind: The C++ Engine Core of InternLM/lmdeploy

entry.content:
Our first visit to InternLM/lmdeploy stayed above the waterline: the CLI, the lite quantization toolkit, the OpenAI-compatible server, and the fork where a request picks either the readable PyTorch engine or the compiled TurboMind core. This visit goes under the waterline, into the C++ half that EuroSys-grade numbers were built on. The questions here are the classic serving-engine questions — where do requests wait, who decides what runs next, how are KV-cache pages handed out and reused — answered with a design that is unusually clean: one engine thread that owns all mutable state, a scheduler that plans several steps ahead of the GPU, and a two-level block system where logical sequences borrow from pooled physical pages. As always, this is an educational walk through published source, Apache-2.0 licensed, on the main branch.

The design decision everything else hangs on is single-threaded ownership. Instead of locks sprinkled through the request path, TurboMind gives the engine one internal thread that pops from a Gateway, and everything else — Python, signal delivery, result forwarding — talks to that thread through queues. Reading the loop below is therefore the most direct way to understand the whole system.

The TurboMind core: the Python TurboMind class reaches through the _turbomind pybind module into the Engine; requests arrive via the Gateway, the Engine's internal thread validates, accepts, cancels and retires them, the Scheduler plans against block pools and a prefix trie, and the ModelExecutor consumes prepared BatchData on its own thread.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • The Python side is TurboMind: it loads weights, calls _create_engine, and hands out per-stream instances from create_instance.
  • The boundary is a pybind module: PYBIND11_MODULE exposes engine handles, request structs, and even multimodal inputs, with config classes auto-generated via a for_each trick at line 379.
  • Gateway is the doorsill: push and pop for requests, cancel for aborts, and a dedicated signal thread so notifications never block the caller.
  • The engine loop at Engine::Impl::InternalThreadEntry is the whole scheduling brain in one while-true.
  • The Scheduler plans each step: admission, prefix matching, resume versus continue, publication.
  • Blocks live in two pools — CacheBlock physical pages managed by CacheBlockPool, and LogicalBlock sequences that borrow them.

The bridge and the boundaries

Between Python and C++ sits more than a translator. The bind.cpp module defines three worlds: engine handles, the request vocabulary — requests, sequences, signals, multimodal inputs — and configuration. The configuration part is the most elegant: C++ config structs register their own fields, so a helper at lines 379 through 390 can expose every option to Python without a hand-written def per attribute — add a field to the struct and the binding follows. Multimodal inputs get first-class treatment too, with per-model item types such as QwenVitItem carrying grid dimensions and token spans, and tensor data crossing by dlpack capsule rather than by copy. On the Python side, TurboMind.init resolves the model source, _process_weights and _create_weight move tensors into the layout the kernels expect, and runtime weight updates or sleep/wakeup travel the same bridge through update_params and wakeup.

The Gateway deserves a closer look because it is the only object on the hot path that Python threads touch concurrently. push enqueues a request and wakes the signal thread; pop drains it under a free-slot budget, optionally blocking; notify is how the engine thread talks back — signals for finished, failed, or cancelled requests are handed to a separate signal thread so that a slow consumer of results never stalls the engine loop itself. Cancellation is also asynchronous: cancel marks a request, and the engine observes it in its own time, which is why the loop below has an explicit Cancel step rather than an interrupt.

The engine loop, one thread to rule the batch

InternalThreadEntry starts with pinning chores — CUDA device, a stream, allocators — then enters the loop that is the engine. Only rank zero talks to the Gateway: the pop at line 797 requests as many free slots as the batch can offer and blocks only when the batch is completely empty, a detail that keeps idle GPUs from spinning hot. The popped requests pass Validate, which checks everything the scheduler would otherwise discover mid-step — token limits, session resumption, multimodal payload shapes — and rejects early with per-request signals. Tensor-parallel ranks then synchronize at line 804 only when the batch is empty, and the full request set is broadcast so every rank runs the identical step.

The body of the iteration is a fixed order that reads like a checklist: Accept turns validated requests into sequences, Cancel applies aborts, gateway notify flushes the resulting signals, Retire frees finished sequences, and only then — with the active count re-reduced across data-parallel groups — does Schedule run. Two quiet guardians follow: FailStalledHeadOfLine catches the case where a queue head cannot fit and everything behind it starves, and cache-stats logging is throttled so observability never becomes load. The ordering matters: because retire precedes schedule, freed pages are reusable in the very same step.

The Scheduler: admission, prefixes, and partial siblings

Where the engine loop is a metronome, the Scheduler is the strategist. Each pass builds a ScheduleState and walks three phases. Required admission at line 1105 handles sequences already holding resources; optional admission at line 1219 brings new prompts in only if that cannot hurt anyone admitted. Prompt admission itself is where the KV cache gets interesting: AdmitPrompt ensures the sequence has blocks, then MatchPrompt walks the prompt against the prefix trie to find already-materialized blocks, and IndexMissingBlocks decides what must still be computed.

The subtle machinery is for shared and resumed sequences. PlanResume rehydrates a sequence from a stored session, SetupPartialSiblings splits a shared prefix where two requests diverge mid-block, and a trio — SetProducers, CheckProducers, MarkProduced — tracks which in-flight sequence will fill a block that others want, so cache reuse does not have to wait for a sequence to finish. Publication of checkpoint blocks is planned separately at PlanPublication, with a clamp that keeps a forward pass from outrunning its context. The step ends with ReplayMemory applying the plan to the block system and CommitResults handing tokens back.

Underneath the scheduler sits a small object system with real engineering in it. A LogicalBlockPtr and a CacheBlockPtr are reference-counted handles that know their pools, so release paths are exception-safe by construction. The physical pool answers the classic eviction question cheaply: SortedBlocks produces candidates in reuse-friendly order, and a Stamp computed over a set of blocks gives the trie a fingerprint to index. Lifecycle is explicit rather than implicit: Invalidate drops a block whose owner rewrote it, Deallocate returns memory to the allocator, and the logical pool’s Recycle fires the trie-erase callback that keeps the prefix index honest — the comment there even notes the pool deliberately stays prefix-agnostic.

The detail view: Python frontend and pybind bridge on the left; the engine tier of Gateway, engine loop, request structs, and BatchData; the scheduler tier with block pools, the prefix trie, and the block implementation file; the memory layer of pages and slabs underneath; and the ModelExecutor thread on the right.

Walking the detail diagram, a token’s journey touches every tier. The request struct itself is compact — Request carries inputs and a generation config, Sequence is the long-lived state, and CacheCopy records when a shared physical block must be duplicated before divergence. The block pools are pooled twice over: LogicalBlockPool recycles logical objects through a callback that erases the sequence from the prefix trie on recycle, while physical pages come from PageAllocator and the pool storage itself is slab-allocated so steady-state serving never wakes the general-purpose heap. On the other end, ModelExecutor runs its own internal thread with a Run that consumes the BatchData the engine filled — container structs like ResolvedCopy carry the block copies that must happen before attention reads.

Splitting the engine thread from the executor thread is not ceremony; it is latency hiding. The scheduler can plan step N+1 — including block allocation and copies — while the GPU is still finishing step N inside the model, and the two only meet at the BatchData hand-off. The same separation protects the reverse path: interrupts such as Interrupt mark a sequence for the engine to observe at a step boundary, and Finalize runs cleanup once the executor has drained, so a cancelled request never frees memory that attention kernels are still reading. It is the same discipline that made the single-threaded engine safe in the first place, applied one layer down.

From Install to Your First Model

Install is pip install lmdeploy, then lmdeploy serve api_server <model> picks TurboMind by default. What this tour adds is the operational reading: create_instance per stream is cheap because the engine, not the instance, owns state; the schedule metrics surfaced by get_schedule_metrics are the engine’s own counters about admission and cache pressure, worth watching before raising max_batch_size; and prefix reuse is automatic — the trie and producer tracking above are why repeated system prompts do not multiply prefill cost.

Honest limits: this walk covered the orchestration core, not the kernels — attention, MoE, and the linear layers under models/llama are their own mountain, and the PyTorch engine shares none of this C++ machinery. We read, not benchmarked; the design claims here are structural. And the engine thread model is a real contract: user code that blocks inside callbacks stalls the whole batch, which is precisely why the Gateway keeps its signal thread. For placement in the ecosystem, vLLM and SGLang solve the same block-management problem in Python, TensorRT-LLM splits the role across MPI processes, and OpenVINO shows what one-graph-per-stream looks like without any server at all. TurboMind’s answer — one thread, one plan, pooled pages — is the most conservative and arguably the easiest to reason about under load.
entry.summary: A second source tour of InternLM/lmdeploy, this time inside the TurboMind C++ core: the Gateway that ships requests across the pybind boundary, the Engine's internal thread, the Scheduler's admission and prefix-reuse machinery, pooled logical and cache blocks, and the ModelExecutor thread that turns a BatchData into a forward pass.

entry.title: MIGraphX Source Tour: The AMD Graph Compiler That Turns ONNX Into HIP Kernels

link.title: MIGraphX Source Tour: The AMD Graph Compiler That Turns ONNX Into HIP Kernels

entry.content:
NVIDIA users get a dizzying menu of inference stacks — we have toured TensorRT-LLM, vLLM, and FlashInfer on that side of the fence. On AMD’s ROCm platform the answer to “how does an ONNX model become fast” is more concentrated: most roads run through MIGraphX, the graph compiler inside the ROCm stack. It is not a server like Triton Inference Server and not a kernel library like FlashInfer; it is a compiler with a familiar shape — frontend, IR, optimization passes, target-specific codegen — and a runtime thin enough that the compiled artifact can be saved to disk and executed without ever seeing the original model again.

The mental model that makes the whole repository click: a program is built once as a graph of ops, then each compile target — gpu, cpu, or ref — receives the graph and answers the same two questions: which passes transform it, and what concrete code runs each instruction. That division is what lets the same program object serve a Radeon GPU through HIP code objects, a server CPU through oneDNN, and a portable reference implementation used for correctness checks. Readers of our TVM and Executorch tours will recognize the compiler-not-runtime philosophy; MIGraphX differs mainly in betting everything on one vendor’s hardware and libraries.

The overview map below follows a model file from left to right: the ONNX frontend fills a module, the program drives passes through the pass manager, each target contributes its own pass sequence, and the GPU path bottoms out in codegen that mixes MIOpen plans, hipBLASLt GEMMs, and Just-In-Time-compiled pointwise kernels.

Overview of MIGraphX: the ONNX parser and its op registry build the module IR; program and pass_manager coordinate optimization; three registered targets (gpu, cpu, ref) each supply passes, with the GPU path ending in HipRTC and library-backed codegen; load_save and the driver complete the toolchain.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • The onnx_parser, L631 walks a GraphProto, looking every node type up in the op_parser registry, L37 that the several dozen parse_*.cpp files self-register into.
  • Everything lands in a module, L369 — an ordered instruction list with named parameters, nested for loops and branches — and modules live inside a program, L380 whose compile() is the front door to all optimization.
  • The pass_manager, L240 executes whichever passes the chosen target requests, and register_target, L56 is the name-to-target map those requests resolve against.
  • The GPU target (target.cpp, L359) assembles a five-stage pass sequence ending in compile_ops, L985, where actual kernel code gets generated or fetched.
  • Around the compiler, load_save, L61 persists compiled programs to MXR files and the migraphx-driver, L1143 provides run, perf, and verify commands from the command line.

A Frontend That Speaks Fluent ONNX

The ONNX path starts at parse_from, L314, which loads the protobuf and hands the graph to parse_graph. Each ONNX operator type has a dedicated handler — from parse_attention to parse_convolution — registered at static-initialization time into the map guarded by register_op_parser, L37. That design matters more than it looks: adding support for a new ONNX op means adding one file with one registration call, and the registry never changes. Tensor initializers become literals via parse_tensor, L870, subgraphs become nested modules, and opset versioning is resolved before any instruction exists.

By the time parsing ends, the model is no longer ONNX at all — it is MIGraphX’s own IR: instructions referencing ops like convolution, dot, and softmax with MIGraphX shape objects attached. This is the layer where our ONNX format and KTransformers tours ended; MIGraphX is where the next step usually starts on ROCm. It is also deliberately decoupled: the ONNX support builds as its own library, so a caller who constructs programs programmatically — the way our ONNX Runtime tour showed for its own ORT format — never links the parser at all.

The Pass Factory: One IR, Many Transformations

Optimization in MIGraphX is a flat list of small passes, and the pass_manager’s run_passes, L240 applies each one to every module in the program, with a tracer for debugging and dead-code elimination inserted between stages. A few passes carry most of the weight. propagate_constant, L81 evaluates constant subgraphs and replaces them with literals. dead_code_elimination, L38 prunes anything no longer referenced — you see it invoked dozens of times in the GPU target’s source because every transformation can orphan instructions. fuse_pointwise, L487 chains elementwise ops into single fused instructions, which later become one kernel launch instead of five.

Two passes handle the less glamorous but equally decisive problems. schedule, L533 partitions instructions across concurrent hardware streams so independent branches of the graph execute in parallel. memory_coloring, L300 assigns offsets in one shared scratch buffer so tensors with disjoint lifetimes reuse the same memory — on a 16 GB card this pass often decides whether a large model fits at all. Because all of this operates on the target-neutral IR, the CPU and reference targets get the same benefits for free.

Inside the GPU Target’s Five-Stage Compile

The GPU target is where MIGraphX earns its complexity budget, and target.cpp, L359 is the file to read. Its factory object (defined at L177) assembles five named stages: dynamic-shape handling, a required stage of normalization and quantization cleanups (L198), an optimization/rewrite stage (L231), a fusion stage (L266), and the backend stage (L293) that actually produces code. What is striking is how hardware-aware the wiring is — the source checks the gfx generation to decide whether FP8 uses OCP or FNUZ intrinsics, whether BF16 needs promotion, and which rewrites apply.

The backend stage is a relay race. fuse_ops uses declarative matchers to catch patterns like conv-plus-bias-plus-relu and rewrite them into fused ops (the apply at L452). compile_miopen, L68 hands convolutions and pooling to MIOpen’s plan-finding machinery, while compile_hipblaslt, L46 resolves GEMMs through hipBLASLt with heuristic algorithm selection. Whatever neither library covers falls to compile_ops, L985, the codegen dispatcher whose compile plans (L432) and compile manager (L774) choose between generating source via HipRTC at compile time, loading prebuilt code objects, or consulting the persistent binary_cache, L131 so a second run of the same model skips compilation entirely.

The generated-code path is the most interesting. The JIT compilers in src/targets/gpu/jit/ interpolate C++ templates — pointwise.cpp’s kernel template, L38 is a string containing #include <migraphx/kernels/pointwise.hpp> plus placeholders — and the pointwise_compiler, L60 fills in the transformer expressions per op. The included headers, like pointwise.hpp, L54, are a full header-only device kernel library written to be #included inside generated source. The result is wrapped in a code_object_op, L76 that launches the compiled kernel at eval time. For deployment, hipgraphify, L255 can capture the whole launch sequence into HIP graphs, cutting per-launch CPU overhead the same way CUDA graph capture does on the NVIDIA side.

Ref, CPU, and the Art of Verification

Two smaller targets give the project its testing culture. The reference target (ref/target.cpp) implements every op with portable scalar code — slow, but unambiguous. The CPU target maps generic ops onto oneDNN through cpu/lowering.cpp’s cpu_apply, L306, which rewrites dot, convolution, and elementwise ops into their dnnl:: counterparts (with native fallbacks like cpu_op, L135), and cpu/dnnl.cpp, L80 converts MIGraphX shapes into oneDNN memory descriptors. This is the same runtime-of-record pattern our DeepSpeed and llama.cpp tours met from the training and kernel sides, here serving correctness rather than speed.

The payoff lives in the driver: migraphx-driver verify (main.cpp, L1004) runs the same program on two targets and diffs the outputs, with --reduce and --bisect modes that shrink a failing graph to the minimal instruction pair that diverges. For compiler work that is a superpower — numerical bugs become small reproducible cases instead of full-model mysteries.

From Install to Your First Model

On a ROCm machine the C++ library plus Python wheel install through the platform packages, and from there the driver does the teaching:

migraphx-driver perf resnet50.onnx --iterations 100
migraphx-driver run resnet50.onnx --input @0 1 3 224 224
migraphx-driver perf resnet50.onnx --gpu

perf compiles, then reports per-instruction and end-to-end timings using the loop in perf.cpp’s time_run, L143. The compiled program saves to an MXR file — save, L61 writes the serialized instruction stream, shapes, and weights — and loading MXR later skips both parsing and compilation. Programmatically, the C API mirrors the C++ core: migraphx_program_compile, L2430 and migraphx_program_run, L2516 are the two calls most embedders live in, and the Python bindings in the same directory wrap them so import migraphx gives you the same program/parameter_map interface.

Honest Limits and Where MIGraphX Fits

Limits first. MIGraphX is ROCm-first: every interesting codegen decision assumes HIP, MIOpen, and hipBLASLt exist, so it is the wrong tool for a heterogeneous fleet that includes NVIDIA or Intel accelerators — that is what the ONNX Runtime and MLC-LLM abstraction layers are for. Model coverage tracks its ONNX op registry: a model using an unregistered op fails at parse time, and while the registry is broad, exotic new transformer ops can trail the research curve by weeks. The LLM story is real but narrower than on NVIDIA — inference serving for chat-scale deployments on AMD typically flows through it via the ROCm builds of vLLM and SGLang, which we covered in the SGLang tour, rather than through MIGraphX’s own serving surface, which does not really exist.

As for fit: MIGraphX is the right read (and tool) when you deploy ONNX models on AMD GPUs and want a compiled, cacheable artifact — the MXR path — or when you are debugging why a model is slow on ROCm and need per-instruction timings plus a reference target to diff against. Between the pass factory, the five-stage GPU compile, and the verify workflow, it is also simply one of the best study objects in the open-source compiler space: small enough to read whole, honest enough to test itself, and opinionated enough to teach you what a graph compiler actually decides. For the serving layer that sits on top, our inference overview maps the remaining territory.
entry.summary: A guided walk through AMD's MIGraphX compiler: the ONNX frontend, the program/module IR, the pass machinery, and the five-stage GPU codegen that ends in MIOpen, hipBLASLt, and HipRTC-generated kernels.
